title: Preventing Misfueling: Keeping Jet A Out of Piston Engines
angle: Why misfueling still happens, the physical barriers (J-spout, filler restrictors), the paper and verbal checks, the airplanes that break the rules of thumb (diesel pistons, turboprops, conversions), and what to do after.
facts: Avgas filler restrictors limit the opening to about 60 mm; U.S. jet nozzles are a flattened J-spout that won't fit (AOPA, Flying; verified 2026-10-11).
Some turbine helicopters (some AStar models) need a smaller nozzle; some piston-to-turbine STC conversions keep the original filler (verified).
1980s misfuelings in turbocharged pistons were traced to 'turbo' read as 'turbine' (AOPA, verified).
NATA's free Safety 1st General Aviation Misfueling Prevention Program (2016), updated 2023 for unleaded grades and UL94 in 100-octane airplanes (verified).
In one fatal accident the line worker rotated the nozzle to fit the filler neck (AIN, 2019; verified).
avgrav: Gravity tells Jet A (about 37 to 51 API) from 100LL (about 65 to 68) in a sample; the range color flags a 100LL sample entered as Jet A; records per truck.
avoid: Specific placard colors (API/EI 1542 is paywalled); claiming gravity catches small contamination.

title: Why Crews Ask for the Fuel's Density: Uplift Checks Explained
angle: The uplift check (metered volume times density versus the gauges), why the density has to match the metered temperature, a worked example, and what to give the crew.
facts: Sample Jet A 43.79 API at 60°F, 806.8 kg/m³ at 15°C; 5,000 gal at 85°F is 4,936.3 net gal, 33,182.9 lb, about 15,050 kg; uncorrected 33,611 lb, 428 lb (194 kg) high, 1.3% (avgrav-math.js).
avgrav: Volume in gallons or liters, weight in lb or kg, density at 15°C and SG at 60°F, the Already corrected to 60°F toggle for compensated meters, saved records for callbacks.

title: Winter at the FBO: Heavier Gallons, Water, and Icing Inhibitor
angle: Cold fuel weighs more per metered gallon (table), water coming out of solution and frozen sump drains, FSII basics, static in dry air, cold-weather habits.
facts: Sample Jet A (6.722 lb/gal at 60°F): lb per metered gal 6.637 at 85°F, 6.790 at 40°F, 6.858 at 20°F, 6.925 at 0°F; about 0.5% per 10°F; 100LL about 0.7% per 10°F (avgrav-math.js).

FSII is usually DiEGME (Prist); injected during uplift at 0.10 to 0.15% by volume as the aircraft documents require; pouring it in afterward doesn't mix, it sinks; many trucks switch injection on and off (SKYbrary, Prist literature; verified).
avgrav: Weight from the real temperature instead of a flat 6.7, notes for sump and FSII, the Apple Watch app in the cold.
avoid: Deicing fluid procedures; claiming which aircraft need FSII.
